The election was decided by ninety-one votes. Ninety-one. In a district of forty thousand registered voters. The recount took two weeks. Lawyers descended from the capital. Both candidates claimed victory. The county clerk, a woman named Dorothy Fenn, worked around the clock. She hand-counted ballots in a windowless room with two assistants. She found three errors. None changed the outcome. The winner was a twenty-eight-year-old teacher. The loser was a three-term incumbent. Voter turnout was thirty-four percent. That means two-thirds of the electorate stayed home and let ninety-one people decide their future. Democracy is not an abstraction. It is arithmetic. Every vote is a brick in the wall. Skip enough bricks and the wall collapses. Dorothy Fenn knows this better than anyone. She has counted every brick for twenty years.
